newsitem.title: USA: U.S. challenges nations on automobile trade policy.
newsitem.headline: U.S. challenges nations on automobile trade policy.

text.p: The United States targeted four nations for investigations on charges of unfair trade practices Tuesday and hailed progress with Japan to deregulate its insurance industry.
Brazil, Indonesia and Australia face investigation for programmes that affect carmakers. Argentina was challenged for excessively high tariffs on imported textiles, apparel and footwear.

At a news conference, Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said an interim agreement with Japan on insurance was "a positive step" but did not meet the U.S. goal of deregulation of Japan's life and non-life insurance sectors.

The interim agreement, announced earlier in the day by Japanese Finance Minister Wataru Kubo, set a December 15 deadline for a comprehensive settlement. It also delayed until 1997 entry by Japanese subsidiaries into the so-called third sector, which has been a profitable niche for foreign firms.
Personal accident, sickness and nursing care insurance were part of the "third sector."
In the interim pact, Japan agreed to allow sales of automobile insurance directly to consumers by mail or telephone, the trade representative said.
Barshefsky called that a "down payment" by Japan on primary sector deregulation.

She also delayed imposition of sanctions in another dispute, involving heavy electrical equipment, because Germany had agreed to open its domestic market. Barshefsky was to meet German Economic State Secretary Lorenz Schomerus on Thursday to discuss details.

Argentina, Australia, Brazil and Indonesia would be subject to investigations under the so-called Section 301 U.S. trade law that allows retaliation against unfair practices. Australia, Argentina and Indonesia also would be subject of a U.S. complaint to the World Trade Organisation.

"In light of the importance of the U.S. auto industry to the U.S. economy, eliminating foreign barriers to U.S. exports of autos and auto parts is of vital importance to the industry's economic growth and to U.S. national economic interests," Barshefsky said.
-- Indonesian policies that grant tax and tariff benefits to "national car" makers based on the percentage of domestic content -- local parts and labour -- in their vehicles;
-- Brazil's policy of reducing tariffs on imported cars if automakers export a sufficient volume of domestically made parts and vehicles and promise to meet local content targets;
-- Australian export subsidies on leather used in automobile upholstery;
-- Argentinian tariffs that exceed the 35 percent level permitted by WTO on textiles, apparel and footwear. Argentina was accused of other import barriers that were contrary to WTO rules.
